title: Parallel Computing
markdown:
## What this covers

Given a computation whose pieces do not depend on one another, how do you actually spread it
across more than one core, more than one machine, or a GPU — and how do you decide *which* way to
split it? This chapter assumes you can already write a working single-machine implementation of
the computation in question (this is where Unit 5's material on efficient implementation ends and
this one begins); the concern here is purely how to get more hardware working on it. The running
tool is Python's `Dask`, with a shorter comparison to R's `future` package at the end.

## Why bother: the four ways to go faster

Before turning to parallelism, it is worth placing it among the other ways a computation can be
sped up:

- **better algorithms** — enormously important in many areas of science, but not the subject here;
- **more efficient implementations of a given algorithm** — the subject of Unit 5;
- **faster computers** — this mattered enormously while Moore's Law held for CPU clock speed, and
  matters less now, though GPU hardware is still improving quickly;
- **more computers** — using more CPUs, more GPU threads, or more compute nodes for a single
  computation. That is this unit's subject.

## Embarrassingly parallel problems

The tools in this chapter only apply when the iterations of a calculation can be carried out
completely independently, with no communication needed between them. This is called an
**embarrassingly parallel (EP)** problem: you can solve it by farming out independent tasks to
separate processes and then collecting the results. In statistics, EP problems are the rule rather
than the exception:

- simulations with many independent replicates,
- bootstrapping,
- stratified analyses,
- random forests,
- cross-validation.

The typical setup is the same code running on different pieces of data (different processes may
need distinct random-number streams — see Scenario 7 below). Doing this requires control over
multiple processes; on a shared cluster with a queueing system, that means requesting a number of
processors and then arranging your job to actually use them.

Ignoring modest overhead, an EP problem with $p$ CPUs can ideally be solved in $1/p$ the time of
the serial version — a **linear speedup** (a speedup of the form $kp$ for a constant $k$). Linear
speedup is the best case, not the typical one; the rest of the chapter is largely about the ways
real hardware and real scheduling fall short of it.

## The vocabulary of parallel hardware

A personal computer usually has more than one processor chip, and each chip usually has more than
one **core**, all sharing the same memory. A cluster or supercomputer instead has many **nodes**,
each essentially its own computer with its own processor(s) and its own memory — communication
between a processor and its own memory is much faster than communication between processors
belonging to different nodes. (Lawrence Berkeley Lab's Perlmutter supercomputer, as an example, has
3072 CPU-only nodes and 1792 GPU nodes, roughly 500,000 CPU cores in total, 512 GB of memory per
node, and 2.3 PB of memory overall.) For most of this chapter the distinction between multiple
chips and multiple cores on one chip doesn't matter — what matters is whether processes share
memory or not.

Some terms recur throughout:

- **process**: an instance of a program executing on a machine; a program may start several at
  once, ideally no more than there are cores available.
- **worker**: a process carrying out part of the parallelized computation (used interchangeably
  with *process*).
- **task**: an individual unit of computation; each worker executes one or more tasks.
- **thread**: a path of execution *within* a process. The operating system sees a multi-threaded
  process as one process, but its threads behave like lightweight processes and, ideally, one
  wants as many cores available as processes-plus-threads combined.
- **forking**: spawning child processes that start out identical to the parent (same code, same
  data) but have their own process ID and, eventually, their own memory. If an object is never
  modified, a forked child can go on referring to the parent's copy rather than duplicating it.
- **scheduler**: the software managing users' jobs on a cluster (Slurm is a common one) — not to be
  confused with the parallel-backend "scheduler" concept in Dask, discussed below.
- **load-balanced**: every core taking part in a computation stays busy for the whole run.
- **sockets**: the communication mechanism some of R's parallel tools use to talk to worker R
  processes they start.

## Shared memory versus distributed memory

Leaving GPUs aside, there are two basic flavors of parallelism.

**Shared memory**: multiple cores access the same memory, so there is no need to pass messages
between machines. But unless you are using true threading (or, in some cases, forked processes),
objects are still *copied* when a new process is created to do part of the work — sharing physical
memory does not automatically mean sharing the objects your code creates. With threading, several
threads genuinely operate on the same object without copying it, though the programmer then has to
avoid threads clobbering memory that other threads are using (largely not something you have to
manage by hand in Python or R). This chapter covers two shared-memory approaches: threaded linear
algebra, and multicore task parallelism (via Dask/`future`).

If you watch CPU usage (e.g. `top`) on a process running threaded code, you'll see it using more
than 100% of a CPU — a sign that one process is genuinely occupying more than one core, as opposed
to appearing as several separate processes. (This is a different phenomenon from *hyperthreading*,
where the operating system is shown two apparent cores for one physical core.)

**Distributed memory**: separate nodes, each with its own memory, requiring messages to be passed
between them. The standard protocol is MPI (e.g. `openMPI`). Several Python and R packages wrap
MPI, but this chapter only covers distributed-memory parallelism through Dask, which does not use
MPI at all.

## GPUs

GPUs (Graphics Processing Units) were built to render graphics quickly by running a very large
number of simple operations in parallel; **GPGPU** (general-purpose GPU) computing reuses that
capability for computation in general. Most users don't program the GPU directly, but rely on
software that has already been written to exploit it — machine learning frameworks such as
TensorFlow and PyTorch, or auto-parallelizing packages such as JAX. Computation on the GPU runs in
**kernels**, functions launched onto the device; the overall program still runs on the CPU, handing
off the computationally heavy pieces. GPUs (and similar devices such as TPUs) are accordingly
sometimes called *co-processors*.

GPU memory is physically separate from main memory, so two practical rules follow: avoid moving
large amounts of data back and forth between CPU and GPU memory, and avoid launching many small
kernels relative to the amount of work each one does, since launching a kernel itself carries
overhead.

## Other approaches, briefly

**Spark and Hadoop** implement distributed-memory computation using the MapReduce approach
(covered in Unit 7, not here). **Cloud computing** (AWS EC2, Google Compute Engine, Azure) rents
virtual machines by usage: you choose the OS, the number of cores, install what you need, and treat
the machine as your own — or assemble several virtual machines into your own virtual cluster and
run platforms such as Spark on top.

## Choosing a parallelization strategy

Before picking a tool, it helps to think through a few considerations: how much memory will the
various processes use, how much data has to be communicated between them, how much latency (delay)
is there in that communication or in starting a worker, and how much does one process have to wait
on another.

From those considerations come some working principles.

**One machine or many?** If the computation fits on the cores of a single node, that will usually
be faster than spreading the same (or even somewhat more) cores across multiple nodes — a problem
that looks like it needs Spark or Hadoop because of its size may in fact run much faster on one
machine with enough memory. That said, if the computation genuinely will not fit in one node's
memory, distributed memory is required.

**What level do you parallelize at?** With nested loops, you generally only want to parallelize at
one level (though later in this chapter there are tools for more than one). Watch for conflicts
with threaded linear algebra happening *inside* the loop you're parallelizing — usually you want to
parallelize the outer loop and not also let each iteration use a threaded BLAS, and usually the
outer loop is the natural level to parallelize.

**Balancing overhead against keeping cores busy.** Too few tasks, especially if they take
noticeably different amounts of time, leaves some cores idle and the computation poorly
load-balanced. Too many tasks, each individually quick, means the overhead of starting and
stopping each one dominates.

**Static or dynamic task assignment?** Should the tasks going to a given worker be decided in
advance (*prescheduling*, i.e. *static* allocation), or should tasks be handed out one at a time,
as each worker finishes its previous one (*dynamic* allocation)? With 6 tasks and 3 workers,
prescheduling might give worker 1 tasks {1,4}, worker 2 tasks {2,5}, worker 3 tasks {3,6}, decided
before anything runs; dynamic allocation instead starts worker 1 on task 1, worker 2 on task 2,
worker 3 on task 3, and whichever worker finishes first — not necessarily worker 1 — picks up task
4, and so on. Roughly: many tasks of similar length favor prescheduling, to cut down on
communication; few tasks, or tasks with highly variable running time, favor dynamic allocation, to
protect load balance. (In R, `future_lapply` exposes this via `future.scheduling` and
`future.chunk.size`; `mclapply()` exposes it via `mc.preschedule`.) Scenario 4 below works this
out with a concrete example.

## Dask: separating "what" from "how" and "where"

Dask (like R's `future` and Python's `ray`) is built around one central idea: separate the
specification of *what* to parallelize, in your code, from *how and where* the parallelization
actually runs — the **backend**. The same code should run, unmodified, whether the "backend" is a
handful of cores on your laptop or a hundred nodes on a cluster; changing the backend should be a
one-line change, not a rewrite.

You control this by setting the **scheduler**:

```python
import dask
dask.config.set(scheduler='processes', num_workers = 4)
```

| Type | Description | Multi-node | Copies of objects made? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `synchronous` | not in parallel (serial) | no | no |
| `threads` | threads within the current Python session | no | no |
| `processes` | separate background Python sessions | no | yes |
| `distributed` | Python sessions across multiple nodes | yes | yes |

Two caveats on this table. Because of Python's Global Interpreter Lock, pure Python code generally
does *not* parallelize under the `threads` scheduler — but computation inside numpy arrays, pandas
data frames, or other C/C++/Cython-backed code does. And the `distributed` scheduler is entirely
usable on a single machine such as a laptop; the Dask documentation credits it with a diagnostic
dashboard and better handling of when copies actually need to be made, and it is required if you
want to use Dask's parallel `map` (Scenario 3 below).

**Getting your data to the workers.** Dask is generally good at noticing which packages and global
variables your parallelized code needs, and shipping them to the workers without you asking. In the
example below, both `numpy` and the global `n` are picked up automatically:

```python
import dask
dask.config.set(scheduler='processes', num_workers = 4, chunksize = 1)

import numpy as np
n = 10

@dask.delayed
def myfun(idx):
   return np.random.normal(size = n)

tasks = []
p = 8
for i in range(p):
    tasks.append(myfun(i))       # add a lazy task

results = dask.compute(tasks)    # compute all in parallel
```

The `@delayed` decorator flags a function to run lazily under Dask; you could instead leave the
function undecorated and wrap each call individually as `dask.delayed(myfun)(i)`, which has the
advantage of leaving you free to call `myfun` normally elsewhere. In other contexts and languages
you may instead have to *export* variables and packages to the workers explicitly — Dask usually
saves you that step.

## Case studies

The rest of the chapter works through the scenarios above one at a time, in increasing order of how
much of the machinery above they need.

### Scenario 1: fitting a single model

**Specific scenario:** fit one statistical or machine-learning model, such as a random forest or a
regression, to your data. **General scenario:** parallelizing a single task.

**1A — built-in parallelism.** Many methods already know how to use multiple cores; you just need
to find the argument that turns it on. Scikit-learn's `RandomForestClassifier`, for instance, takes
an `n_jobs` argument. Look for an argument containing a word like *threads*, *processes*, *cores*,
*cpus*, or *jobs*.

**1B — threaded linear algebra.** If a method does linear algebra on large matrices, Python and R
delegate that to the **BLAS** and **LAPACK** libraries (the basic linear-algebra operations,
written in Fortran or C). A fast, *threaded* BLAS — Intel's MKL, the open-source OpenBLAS, or
Apple's Accelerate/vecLib on a Mac — can use multiple cores automatically for a single large linear
algebra operation, provided the shell variable `OMP_NUM_THREADS` isn't set to 1 (`VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS`
on a Mac, `MKL_NUM_THREADS` under MKL). For example, on a $6000\times 6000$ Cholesky decomposition:

```python
import numpy as np
import time

x = np.random.normal(size = (6000, 6000))

start_time = time.time()
x = np.dot(x.T, x)
U = np.linalg.cholesky(x)
elapsed_time = time.time() - start_time
```

with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` (a single thread), this took about 6.6 seconds; with 8 threads
available, about 3 seconds — a real speedup, but closer to 2x than to the 8x linear speedup an
embarrassingly parallel problem could in principle reach. Threaded linear algebra can also fail to
help, or even be slower, for smaller problems, because of the overhead of setting up the parallel
computation and because the parallel algorithm sometimes does strictly more arithmetic than the
serial one.

**1C — GPUs for linear algebra.** Large matrix operations are one of the best use cases for a GPU.
Packages such as PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX can run the same linear-algebra call on CPU or GPU
depending on what hardware is available, dispatching to a different *kernel* (implementation)
underneath:

```python
import torch

gpu = torch.device("cuda:0")
n = 10000
x = torch.randn(n, n, device = gpu)
y = torch.randn(n, n, device = gpu)
z = torch.matmul(x, y)      # ~100-200 ms on the GPU

cpu = torch.device("cpu")
x = torch.randn(n, n, device = cpu)
y = torch.randn(n, n, device = cpu)
z = torch.matmul(x, y)      # ~18 sec on the CPU (2 cores)
```

That's better than a 100x speedup from the GPU — though a fully fair comparison would also account
for the GPU calculation's use of 4-byte (single-precision) floating point, and for exactly how many
CPU cores are being compared against.

**1D — parallelized vectorized calculations.** The same packages also parallelize plain vectorized
array operations, not just linear algebra. Unit 5 showed JAX automatically parallelizing a
vectorized calculation on a large 1-d array across CPU cores; the same code, with a GPU available,
runs automatically on the GPU instead:

```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def myfun_jnp(x):
    return jnp.exp(x) + 3 * jnp.sin(x)

n = 500000000
key = jax.random.key(1)
x_jax = jax.random.normal(key, (n,))
z = myfun_jnp(x_jax).block_until_ready()
```

On one GPU-equipped machine this took about 0.015 seconds on the GPU against about 4.7 seconds on
the CPU — even though the CPU run itself used several threads. (Forcing JAX to ignore an available
GPU and stick to the CPU turns out to be fiddly in practice.)

### Scenario 2: a handful of independent tasks

**Specific scenario:** fit three different models to the same data. **General scenario:**
parallelizing a small number of tasks. The options are to use one core per model, or — if there are
substantially more than three cores and each model itself parallelizes — one node per model,
combining this scenario with Scenario 1.

```python
import dask
import time
import numpy as np

def gen_and_mean(func, n, par1, par2):
    return np.mean(func(par1, par2, size = n))

dask.config.set(scheduler='processes', num_workers = 3, chunksize = 1)
n = 250000000

tasks = [
    dask.delayed(gen_and_mean)(np.random.normal, n, 0, 1),
    dask.delayed(gen_and_mean)(np.random.gamma, n, 1, 1),
    dask.delayed(gen_and_mean)(np.random.uniform, n, 0, 1),
]
results = dask.compute(tasks)
```

(Worth pausing on: why might this *not* give a clean three-fold speedup over the serial version?
The lecture poses this as an open question rather than answering it.)

This introduces three more pieces of vocabulary. `dask.compute` is **synchronous**, also called
**blocking**: the main process waits for it to finish before doing anything else, as opposed to
**asynchronous** (**non-blocking**) execution, where control returns before the workers are done.
And the `chunksize = 1` argument matters: without it, Dask by default groups (*chunks*) tasks
together to cut down on per-task startup overhead, which with only a few tasks defeats the purpose
of parallelizing them at all — the subject of Scenario 4. Finally, `dask.delayed` builds a
**computational graph** describing what depends on what, and only actually runs anything once you
call `compute` — a form of **lazy evaluation**.

### Scenario 3: cross-validation via a parallel map

**Specific scenario:** run a prediction method over 10 cross-validation folds.
**General scenario:** parallelizing many similar tasks with a parallel map.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor

def cv_fit(fold_idx):
    train_idx = folds != fold_idx
    test_idx = folds == fold_idx
    model = RandomForestRegressor()
    model.fit(X.iloc[train_idx], Y[train_idx])
    return model.predict(X.iloc[test_idx])

n_folds = 10
folds = np.random.permutation(np.repeat(np.arange(n_folds), 100))
```

`cv_fit` reaches into the global variables `X`, `Y` and `folds` rather than taking them as
arguments, because a parallel `map` only passes a single argument per call — the fold index (you
could instead bundle the data with the index into one object, but globals are simpler here). A
parallel `map` requires the `distributed` scheduler, which is fine to run on a single machine:

```python
from dask.distributed import Client, LocalCluster
cluster = LocalCluster(n_workers = 2)
c = Client(cluster)

tasks = c.map(cv_fit, range(n_folds))
results = c.gather(tasks)
```

With, say, 4 cores and 10 folds, the tasks don't divide evenly across workers — which is exactly
the situation the next scenario addresses.

### Scenario 4: static versus dynamic allocation

**Scenario:** parallelizing tasks whose running time varies a lot from one to the next — over
prediction methods, say, rather than over folds of similar size.

When tasks take noticeably different amounts of time, you generally don't want them grouped into
batches decided in advance, because a batch might by chance contain several of the slow ones while
another worker's batch is all fast ones and it sits idle once done. Starting tasks one at a time as
work becomes available is **dynamic allocation**. When tasks take about the same time and there are
many of them, batching them (**static allocation** / **prescheduling**) instead avoids the
per-task scheduling overhead — on the order of a millisecond per task.

The lecture works this out with an artificial mix of 4 slow tasks and 12 fast ones. Dask's
`distributed` scheduler always starts each delayed evaluation separately — it is inherently
dynamic, and there is no way to ask it to batch tasks into chunks. The `processes` scheduler, by
contrast, batches by default (chunksize 6), which is static allocation; setting `chunksize = 1`
forces it into dynamic, one-task-at-a-time behavior instead. Exactly which tasks Dask groups into
which chunk under the `processes` scheduler is not fully predictable — rerunning the same code
shows some randomness in the assignment — so a batch can occasionally end up with more than one
slow task in it, which is precisely the imbalance the figure above illustrates. In one comparison,
the default (static, chunksize 6) run and the forced dynamic (chunksize 1) run on the same
artificial workload came out at about the same wall time; the general expectation is still that
dynamic allocation should do better when task times vary, unless the static batches happen to be
well balanced anyway — but dynamic allocation is itself no guarantee of good balance, since it is
still possible for several slow tasks to be picked up back-to-back by the same lucky (or unlucky)
worker. Where each task is genuinely quick and there are many of them, static allocation's lower
overhead is the main reason to prefer it. (In R, prescheduling is the default under the `future`
package.)

### Scenario 5: nested tasks and multiple nodes

**Specific scenario:** an ensemble method such as SuperLearner or Bayesian model averaging, run
over 10 folds with many candidate learners per fold — many more tasks than in Scenario 3, and
naturally organized as nested loops.

**5A — flattening nested loops.** You can always flatten two nested loops into one, indexing by
the combined position:

```python
## original: nested loops
for fold in range(n):
    for method in range(M):
        ...

## flattened
for idx in range(n * M):
    fold, method = idx // M, idx % M
```

Alternatively, rather than flattening the loop itself, you can simply build up the list of delayed
tasks from within the nested loops directly:

```python
for fold in range(n):
    for method in range(M):
        tasks.append(dask.delayed(myfun)(fold, method))
```

(R's `future` package has built-in support for nested parallelization.)

**5B — multiple nodes.** With access to a networked cluster, Dask can start workers across several
machines at once (whether or not the tasks are nested):

```python
from dask.distributed import Client, SSHCluster
cluster = SSHCluster(["host1", "host2", "host2", "host3", "host3"])
# the first host also runs the scheduler process
c = Client(cluster)

tasks = c.map(fun, range(n_tasks))
results = c.gather(tasks)
```

On a Slurm-managed cluster, the list of assigned machine names for a job can be found with
`srun hostname`, repeating the first entry to also account for the scheduler process.

### Scenario 6: avoiding unnecessary copies with large data

**Specific scenario:** a stratified analysis run repeatedly over one very large dataset, where you
want to avoid needlessly copying it.

Even though the cores on one node physically share memory, separate *processes* do not
automatically share objects — the data has to be sent to each process and stored as its own copy.
Instrumenting a toy analysis function to print the memory address of its input and the ID of the
process running it shows this directly:

```python
import os

def do_analysis(i, x):
    print(f"Object id: {id(x)}, process id: {os.getpid()}")
    return np.mean(x)

x = np.random.normal(size = 5*10**7)
dask.config.set(scheduler='processes', num_workers = 4, chunksize = 1)

tasks = [dask.delayed(do_analysis)(i, x) for i in range(8)]
results = dask.compute(tasks)
```

Under the `processes` scheduler, this produced eight distinct object IDs for eight tasks spread
across four processes — a fresh copy *per task*, the worst case, not just one copy per process.
Switching to the `threads` scheduler avoids the copying altogether, since threads within one
process genuinely share the same objects (at the cost of no longer being able to safely have
different tasks modify the data concurrently), and is correspondingly much faster here. The
`distributed` scheduler, wrapping the shared object in `dask.delayed(x)` before passing it, can
give one copy per *worker* instead of one per task — a middle ground — though the scheduler's own
choices about which worker gets which task can be lumpy enough (in one run, every task ended up on
a single worker) to make a clean comparison difficult. Dask separately warns about sending large
data to workers this way and recommends `scatter()` instead; the lecture notes candidly that it
isn't clear exactly how that recommendation differs from `dask.delayed(x)`, and that the warning
persisted even after trying `scatter()`.

### Scenario 7: random numbers across parallel tasks

**Specific scenario:** a simulation study with 1000 replicates, each fitting a couple of models.
**General scenario:** generating random numbers safely when the generation happens in more than
one process at once.

Random numbers on a computer are really a long, deterministic, eventually-repeating sequence;
setting a seed just picks a starting position in it. The risk in parallel is that two processes,
seeded independently, draw from *overlapping* stretches of that sequence — probably unlikely if
neither process draws very many numbers, but genuinely unclear how safe it is in general.

Numpy's `PCG64` and `MT19937` bit generators expose a `jumped()` method that advances the generator
state as if a huge number of draws had already happened ($2^{128}$ for the Mersenne Twister, and
nearly that many for PCG64 — a period the lecture notes finding "quite strange" without a full
explanation for the intuition behind it):

```python
bitGen = np.random.PCG64(1)
bitGen = bitGen.jumped(i)     # jump forward by task index i
rng = np.random.Generator(bitGen)
```

The alternative numpy recommends is `SeedSequence`, which spawns a set of child generators
guaranteed to be well separated from each other:

```python
n_tasks = 10
sg = np.random.SeedSequence(1)
rngs = [np.random.Generator(np.random.PCG64(s)) for s in sg.spawn(n_tasks)]
# pass one element of rngs into each parallel task
```

R's `rlecuyer` package solves the same problem with the L'Ecuyer algorithm, whose period of
$2^{191}$ is divided into subsequences of length $2^{127}$, one per stream.

## A few more practical details

**Do all the work inside one call to `compute`.** Dask does not, in general, keep every piece of a
distributed computation cached in memory, so if a distributed dataset is read from disk, a second
separate call to `compute` may mean reading it from disk all over again. Bundling everything you
need into one computational graph avoids repeating that work:

```python
import dask.dataframe as ddf
air = ddf.read_csv(path + '*.csv.bz2', compression = 'bz2', ...)

# slower: two separate reads of the data from disk
air.DepDelay.min().compute()
air.DepDelay.max().compute()

# faster: one graph, one read
mn, mx = dask.compute(air.DepDelay.max(), air.DepDelay.min())
```

**Controlling thread counts.** Most threaded (OpenMP-based) code respects the `OMP_NUM_THREADS`
environment variable (`VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS` on a Mac, `MKL_NUM_THREADS` under Intel MKL), set
before starting the R or Python session:

```bash
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=4
```

As Scenario 1B showed, more threads is not automatically faster, particularly for small matrices,
because of parallelization overhead and because the parallel algorithm may do more total work than
the serial one. This matters most when you are *also* parallelizing across independent tasks (as
in Scenarios 2–5): it is usually better to give each task a single BLAS thread
(`OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`) and let the outer, task-level parallelism use all the cores, rather than
letting each task's linear algebra try to thread as well.

## R's `future` package, briefly

R has its own version of the same idea, developed as an alternative to older tools such as
`parallel::parLapply`, `parallel::mclapply`, and `foreach` without a backend. (`partools` is a
related, more specialized package: it borrows the distributed file system and distributed data
object ideas from Spark/Hadoop while deliberately dropping fault tolerance for very large clusters,
which most statistical uses don't need.)

A **future** is an abstraction for a value that will be available later — the result of an
expression that is either *unresolved* or *resolved*. As with Dask, the point is to separate what
to compute from how and where it runs: you write ordinary-looking code, and a single call to
`plan()` at the top decides the backend.

```r
plan(multisession)
# or, controlling the worker count directly:
plan(multisession, workers = 4)
```

| Type | Description | Multi-node | Copies of objects made? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `multisession` | additional R sessions as workers | no | yes |
| `multicore` | forked R processes as workers | no | not if the object isn't modified |
| `cluster` | R sessions on other machine(s) | yes | yes |

Like Dask, `future` (via the `globals` package) is generally good at detecting which packages and
global variables a parallelized function needs and shipping them to the workers automatically:

```r
library(future); library(future.apply); library(MASS)
plan(multisession)

n <- nrow(geyser)
myfun <- function(idx) sum(geyser$duration) / n   # geyser: from MASS

future_sapply(1:5, myfun)
```

As with Dask, you can also explicitly *export* variables or load packages on the workers when
automatic detection isn't enough.
